extracted.intended_audience: professional geometers, advanced students and readers of the Mathematical Repository (practitioners of synthetic/projective geometry)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for producing and judging synthetic and projective-geometry proofs and ruler-only constructions (especially for conic sections, polygons inscribed/circumscribed, and related loci). Emphasises methods (projection, poles/polars, harmonic division), existence/uniqueness issues, and the need for rigorous demonstration beyond heuristic diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection/perspective as a legitimate heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Use perspective (projection) to indicate and suggest truths about conic sections and associated polygons — the projection of a system of polygons and their circumscribing conics gives corresponding conic representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projection furnishes unquestionable evidence of the truth of theorems when circle-correlatives are known; it is useful as an exploratory or demonstrative device and as an incentive toward finding systematic proofs. However, it may be seen as a 'geometrical trickery' and should be used primarily to guide, not to replace, a rigorous demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide systematic logical proofs beyond projection
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when projection or experimental diagrams make a result evident, one should remount to first principles and give a legitimate, logical proof of the theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagrams and projection are like experiments; they help discover truths but do not substitute for analytic or synthetic proofs. Authors should convert persuasive geometric evidence into formal demonstrations (e.g., coordinate or classical synthetic proofs) and carefully check exceptional cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructions 'by means of straight lines only' (ruler-only constructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer and value constructions that can be carried out using straight lines alone (ruler-only), especially for tasks like circumscribing a triangle about a conic or constructing tangents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a construction claims 'by means of straight lines only', it must explicitly avoid tools beyond the ruler: include constructions for poles, chords of contact, and tangents using only line operations. Provide linear procedures (e.g., use intersections and joins) that produce the required tangents or contact points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of poles and polars (duality principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ the doctrine of poles and polars (the principle of duality) to transform problems into their dual forms and to construct tangents/chords/inscribed/circumscribed polygons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify poles corresponding to given lines, use polars to find contact points and tangents, and exploit duality to derive one construction from another. Explicitly demonstrate the relationships (e.g., pole of a line, polar of a point, intersections determining poles) used in the construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit construction of tangents and polars (include linear algorithms)
rubrics_metrics.description: When tangents (or polars) are required in a construction, give a concrete method to obtain them by straight lines: determine poles, draw secants, locate intersection points that determine polars, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, introduce an arbitrary secant or auxiliary circle where needed (an 'arbitrary circle through two given points' or an arbitrary secant UXY) and describe the linear steps (join, intersect, draw polars) that yield the tangent. Do not leave 'draw the tangents' as an unelaborated step if the construction claims ruler-only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check existence, uniqueness, and special/degenerate cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse and state the conditions under which a construction or theorem is possible, impossible, or indeterminate (e.g., the parity of number of sides, whether the line of poles meets the curve, coincident given lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine particular cases (odd vs even number of polygon sides leading to indeterminacy or impossibility), note when desired intersections lie off the curve, and state when constructions produce identical solutions or none. Explicitly point out degenerate configurations (e.g., three given lines concurrent) and their impact on the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use auxiliary/auxiliary-circle devices to simplify constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce auxiliary elements (e.g., an arbitrary circle through given points instead of a third proportional) to simplify the practical construction and the demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such auxiliary choices often improve both construction and proof; authors should indicate why the auxiliary element is legitimate and show how it reduces complexity (for instance, producing a radical centre or convenient tangency points).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit classical projective properties (Pascal, Brianchon, harmonic division)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use known projective theorems and properties — Pascal's theorem, Brianchon's theorem, harmonic division, chords of contact — as tools in analysis and construction of polygons and tangents on conics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these properties to deduce collinearities, concurrency, and polar relationships (e.g., the three intersections of opposite sides of an inscribed hexagon are collinear). Use harmonic division and related projective invariants to justify steps that involve division of lines or cross-ratio arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide necessary lemmas and elementary geometric facts early
rubrics_metrics.description: State and prove elementary lemmas (e.g., 'a plane section parallel to two opposite edges of a tetrahedron is a parallelogram') that underpin more complex constructions or relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include small, self-contained results that the main construction or proof relies upon; make their hypotheses and conclusions explicit so later substitutions and algebraic manipulations are justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: When possible, supply analytic/coordinate proofs as alternatives for rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Complement synthetic/projective constructions with Cartesian or analytic demonstrations to increase rigor and clarity, particularly for results of Poncelet and others in projective geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate methods or the method of transversals can often render projective theorems amenable to algebraic verification. Where projection-based arguments are used, providing an analytic proof helps detect exceptional cases and confirm generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and make use of classical centers (radical centre, poles of given points)
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructions involve circles and points (e.g., arbitrary circle through two given points), identify centers like the radical centre or poles of lines as key intermediate objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state and use these centers in constructions and proofs (e.g., P is the 'radical centre' of the given circle and two zero-radius circles at two points). This clarifies why certain lines meet or why tangents drawn from constructed points have the required properties.
